# Cloud Native Hackathon kickoff (summary)

Our own short summary of the kickoff themes for the WeMakeDevs Cloud Native Hackathon, Monday 9 November 2026, Salt Lake City, the day before KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 opens. It is not a verbatim transcript.

## The challenge: make conferences easier

KubeCon is huge. A first-timer faces hundreds of sessions across two buildings, a showcase hall full of booths, and thousands of people they have never met. The kickoff asked teams to build something that makes the conference easier to navigate: finding the right talk, finding the right people, and actually meeting them. The best entries help someone on day one, not only power users.

## One day, one cluster per team

Every team gets its own Kubernetes cluster, a virtual cluster on shared hosts, where the team is cluster-admin. Deploys are GitOps: push to main and Argo CD syncs the team namespace. Each team has a fixed resource budget (2 CPU and 4 GiB of requests), so efficient workloads matter. The public URL for every team is routed to a single Service on port 80.

## The sponsors and what they bring

- **Elastic**: Elasticsearch on Elastic Cloud Serverless as the data layer. Semantic search with `semantic_text` and Jina embeddings, hybrid search that fuses keyword and vector results with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), geo queries, aggregations, the inference API for language models, Agent Builder and Workflows.
- **Dash0**: observability built on OpenTelemetry. Send traces, metrics and logs over OTLP and follow a single request across services.
- **Radar**: Radar Cloud shows every team's cluster, its workloads, GitOps state, events and health checks, and exposes an MCP server so coding agents can observe and operate the cluster safely.
- **Gitar and Sonar**: code quality and AI code review on every pull request, with team-defined review rules.

## How projects are judged

Judges look for a working demo on the live URL, real use of the sponsor technologies rather than logos, clear observability of what the app is doing, and something an attendee would actually want to use tomorrow morning. Teams should show the deploy story: a commit, a sync, a healthy rollout.

## Practical advice from the kickoff

Ship the smallest end-to-end slice early, deploy it, then improve it. Keep secrets out of the public repo. Watch the resource budget: a pod over quota stays Pending. Demos are short, so rehearse the path a judge will take from scanning a QR code to seeing a result.

The keynote brings together perspectives on what open infrastructure components agentic systems depend on and how the cloud native ecosystem could evolve to support autonomous agents at scale.

Likely topics include the architectural patterns that distinguish agentic AI workloads from traditional containerized applications, the resource orchestration challenges that arise when agents make dynamic decisions about compute and data access, and the role of Kubernetes primitives in providing scheduling, networking, and state management for agent runtimes. This keynote suits platform engineers evaluating how their Kubernetes clusters will support AI agent deployments, architects designing infrastructure for agentic applications, and contributors to cloud native projects interested in extending the ecosystem to accommodate new AI-driven workload patterns. Likely topics include workload identity mechanisms such as service accounts, SPIFFE and SPIRE frameworks, and how these primitives extend to AI agent workloads. Attendees can expect discussion of attestation techniques that allow a cluster to verify not only what pod is running but also which model, tool chain, or orchestration layer initiated a request. The talk will likely touch on audit logging and observability for agent actions, helping teams answer questions like which decisions were made by an agent versus a human, and how to reconstruct the chain of custody for sensitive operations. Multi-tenancy considerations may also feature, particularly how to isolate agent workloads and prevent privilege escalation when multiple agents or teams share a cluster.

This keynote suits platform engineers, security architects, and DevOps practitioners responsible for Kubernetes security posture, especially those beginning to incorporate AI tooling into their workflows. summary: This session covers attestation-driven admission control in Kubernetes environments, demonstrating how Kyverno policy engine and Common Expression Language work together to validate container image signatures and attestations before allowing workloads into a cluster. The approach emphasizes creating an auditable record of every admission decision, linking security posture to verifiable evidence about image provenance and build integrity. Likely topics include the fundamentals of image signing and attestation workflows in cloud native supply chains, how admission webhooks intercept deployment requests to evaluate policy conditions, the role of CEL in expressing complex attestation validation logic within Kyverno policies, and the structure of attestation payloads that carry cryptographic proof of build provenance or security scan results. The session probably explores how attestation metadata travels alongside container images, the difference between verifying a signature and validating the claims inside an attestation, and how Kyverno matches attestation predicates against cluster policy requirements. It may touch on integration points with signing frameworks, the performance considerations of validating attestations during admission, and how audit logs capture both successful and denied requests with evidence references that satisfy compliance requirements. This session suits platform engineers responsible for hardening Kubernetes admission pipelines, security architects designing supply chain security controls, and DevSecOps teams implementing policy-as-code frameworks that bridge build-time assurances and runtime enforcement. It will benefit those exploring alternatives to simple image signature checks and seeking richer policy models that interrogate attestation content rather than just cryptographic validity. Questions to ask the speakers: How does the attestation verification process handle cases where multiple attestations with conflicting claims are present on the same image? What strategies do you recommend for managing the performance overhead of CEL evaluation and cryptographic operations during high-throughput admission scenarios? How should teams structure their Kyverno policies to evolve attestation requirements over time without breaking existing workloads that lack newer attestation types? What observability or debugging tools help operators troubleshoot denied admissions when attestation validation logic becomes complex?

summary:
This session covers an approach to running Kubernetes nodes in air-gapped virtual private clouds by replacing traditional network-based control plane connectivity with cloud object storage as the communication medium. The talk focuses on environments where nodes have zero outbound network access, presenting an alternative to Konnectivity's gRPC-based tunnel for maintaining the control plane to node link that Kubernetes requires.

Likely topics include the architecture of standard Kubernetes control plane communication patterns, the role of components like Konnectivity in bridging network boundaries, and the constraints imposed by air-gapped or egress-restricted VPC configurations. The session may explore how object storage can serve as an asynchronous message bus for control plane instructions and node status updates, the trade-offs between synchronous gRPC connections and storage-mediated communication, and the implications for latency, reliability, and failure modes. It may also touch on the security and compliance motivations for eliminating egress entirely, the challenges of adapting Kubernetes' expectations around node heartbeats and real-time communication, and the practical implementation details required to make kubelet, kube-proxy, and other node components function without direct network paths to the API server.

This talk suits platform engineers working in highly regulated industries with strict network isolation requirements, security architects evaluating zero-trust or air-gapped deployment models, and infrastructure teams managing multi-cloud or hybrid environments where egress costs or compliance rules make traditional connectivity patterns impractical. It may also interest contributors working on Kubernetes networking or control plane components who are curious about unconventional deployment scenarios and the extensibility of core communication mechanisms.

Questions to ask the speakers: How does the storage-based communication model affect the responsiveness of pod scheduling and lifecycle events compared to a direct gRPC connection? What are the failure scenarios and recovery behaviors when the object storage service itself becomes unavailable or experiences delays? Are there specific workload types or cluster scales where this approach becomes impractical due to latency or throughput limitations? How does this design handle real-time features like kubectl exec or log streaming that typically rely on bidirectional streaming connections?

summary:
This session covers the evolution of internal developer platforms in a landscape increasingly shaped by AI tooling and automation. The talk examines how platform engineering teams can move beyond traditional interface-driven approaches to build systems that understand and act on developer intent, whether that intent comes from human engineers or AI agents. The speaker explores architectural and design patterns that enable platforms to interpret goals rather than simply execute prescribed commands, positioning IDPs as intelligent intermediaries that can reason about requirements and translate them into appropriate infrastructure actions.

Likely topics include the distinction between imperative and declarative platform interfaces, the role of semantic understanding in platform APIs, and how intent-driven design differs from current generation developer portals and service catalogs. The session may explore how large language models and AI agents interact with platform tooling, the importance of observable and auditable intent resolution, and strategies for backward compatibility as platforms adopt richer input models. Concepts such as policy enforcement in intent-based systems, the relationship between platform abstractions and underlying Kubernetes primitives, and the balance between flexibility and guardrails in multi-tenant environments are likely to feature. The talk may also address how platform teams can instrument and measure the effectiveness of intent interpretation, ensuring that automated agents and human developers receive appropriate feedback and that the platform evolves based on actual usage patterns rather than assumptions.

This session suits platform engineers responsible for internal developer experience, architects designing next-generation tooling for cloud native environments, and engineering leaders evaluating how AI tooling will change their delivery processes. It will be valuable for teams currently operating Kubernetes-based platforms who want to understand where the industry is heading and how to prepare their systems for a future where both developers and autonomous agents consume platform services. Those interested in the intersection of developer experience, platform architecture, and emerging AI workflows will find relevant insights.

Questions to ask the speakers: How do you recommend platform teams begin instrumenting intent without over-engineering for speculative AI use cases? What governance and approval models work well when agents rather than humans are making infrastructure requests? How should platforms handle ambiguous or conflicting intent, and what role does human intervention play in those scenarios? What existing open source projects or standards are moving toward intent-driven models that platform teams can adopt today?

The session focuses on how KServe addresses these production concerns for organizations moving beyond experimental deployments.

Likely topics include the architectural patterns for LLM inference serving, including how KServe manages model serving runtimes and coordinates traffic across multiple model replicas or versions. The discussion may explore horizontal pod autoscaling strategies tailored to the unique resource profiles of transformer-based models, which typically require GPU acceleration and exhibit different latency and throughput characteristics than traditional machine learning models. Request-level routing considerations could encompass canary deployments, A/B testing between model versions, and intelligent load balancing that accounts for the stateful nature of some LLM inference patterns. The session might also address multi-tenancy concerns, batch versus streaming inference trade-offs, and how KServe integrates with broader cloud native observability and service mesh tooling to provide visibility into model performance and resource utilization.

summary: This session covers security vulnerabilities in Kubernetes operators that can allow unprivileged users within a namespace to gain unauthorized access to cluster-level or cloud provider administrative privileges through confused-deputy attack patterns. The presentation examines how the architectural design of operators, which typically run with elevated permissions to manage resources across namespaces or interact with external systems, can be exploited when those operators accept input or configuration from namespace-scoped users without sufficient validation or authorization checks. Likely topics include the trust boundaries between namespace-level and cluster-level permissions in Kubernetes, the privilege escalation chains that emerge when operators act on behalf of users with higher privileges than those users possess directly, and the specific code patterns or configuration mistakes that create these vulnerabilities. The session will probably explore how custom resource definitions and operator reconciliation loops can become attack vectors, the role of service accounts and RBAC policies in either enabling or preventing these flaws, and the challenges of designing operators that safely mediate between untrusted user input and privileged operations. Discussion may extend to multi-tenant cluster environments where namespace isolation is critical, the risks posed by operators that interact with cloud provider APIs or infrastructure outside the cluster, and detection strategies for identifying whether existing operators in a cluster contain these vulnerabilities. This talk suits platform engineers responsible for evaluating or deploying third-party operators, security teams auditing Kubernetes environments for privilege escalation risks, and operator developers who need to understand secure design principles for controllers that handle user-provided configuration. It will be particularly relevant for organizations running multi-tenant clusters or those where namespace users should not be able to affect cluster infrastructure or peer namespaces. Questions to ask the speakers: What specific RBAC configurations or admission control policies can effectively prevent these confused-deputy attacks without breaking legitimate operator functionality? Are there automated scanning tools or testing frameworks that can identify vulnerable patterns in operator code before deployment? How should organizations balance the operational convenience of powerful operators against the security risks in environments with varying trust levels? What changes to Kubernetes core APIs or operator frameworks would make it easier to build secure operators by default?

summary:
This session covers the challenge of efficiently moving columnar data to multiple destinations in modern GPU-accelerated workflows without creating redundant copies for each target system. The speakers examine an approach built on Apache Arrow Flight that aims to stream data once and make it available to training pipelines, lakehouse storage, and serving infrastructure simultaneously.

Likely topics include the overhead introduced by traditional data movement patterns where each downstream system requires its own copy of the source data, the architecture of Apache Arrow as an in-memory columnar format optimized for analytical workloads, and how Arrow Flight extends this with a framework for high-performance data transport over the network. The session may explore the characteristics of GPU memory that make naive copying particularly expensive, the role of lakehouse architectures in unifying batch and streaming analytics, and how serving systems for inference benefit from direct access to columnar representations. Attendees might hear about zero-copy techniques, the trade-offs between materialized copies and shared views of data, and how columnar formats align with the tensor operations common in machine learning. The discussion could touch on network bandwidth considerations, serialization costs, and the coordination required to ensure multiple consumers can read from a single stream without blocking one another.

This session suits data engineers building ML pipelines who wrestle with data duplication across training, storage, and inference stages, platform engineers responsible for GPU cluster utilization and cost, and architects designing lakehouse or feature store systems where data movement becomes a bottleneck. It will also interest practitioners working with Apache Arrow or evaluating columnar formats for analytics and ML workloads, as well as teams managing the boundary between data engineering and ML engineering where handoffs often introduce latency and complexity.

Questions to ask the speakers: How does the single-stream approach handle backpressure when one consumer is slower than others, and are there mechanisms to buffer or skip data for lagging targets? What are the practical limits on the number of concurrent consumers reading from one Arrow Flight stream before performance degrades? How does this pattern integrate with existing orchestration tools and lakehouse table formats like Delta Lake or Iceberg that have their own transaction and versioning semantics? What observability or debugging strategies help diagnose issues when data flows to multiple destinations and one fails silently or falls behind?
